title: Taxes Basics

learn.summary: Taxes are most people's largest annual expense, yet the system is widely misunderstood in ways that cause real mistakes — like refusing raises for fear of 'a higher bracket'. The essentials are learnable in an afternoon: how marginal brackets actually apply, what withholding is doing to each paycheck, and where legitimately free filing help lives. Understanding the machinery also inoculates against IRS-impersonation scams.

links.label: Wikipedia: Taxation in the United States

do: Find last year's tax return and locate three numbers: total income, total tax paid, and your effective tax rate (tax divided by income).

children.title: How Brackets Actually Work

learn.summary: The U.S. income tax is marginal: each bracket's rate applies only to the dollars inside that bracket, so 'moving into the 22% bracket' means only your dollars above the threshold are taxed at 22% — everything below keeps its lower rates. A raise can never reduce your take-home pay through brackets alone; believing otherwise is perhaps the single most common tax myth. Your effective rate (total tax / total income) is always lower than your top marginal rate.

do: Using the current IRS bracket table, hand-calculate the tax on a hypothetical $60,000 taxable income bracket by bracket, and compare the effective rate you get to the top marginal rate.

children.title: Withholding Explained

learn.summary: Your employer prepays your estimated tax from each paycheck based on the W-4 form you filed; filing season is just the reconciliation between what was withheld and what you actually owed. A big refund means you overpaid all year — an interest-free loan to the government — while a big bill means you underpaid, which can trigger penalties. The IRS's free Tax Withholding Estimator lets you check the match mid-year and adjust via a new W-4.

do: Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with your latest pay stub and note whether you're on track to owe or be refunded, and by roughly how much.

children.title: Common Misconceptions

learn.summary: Beyond the bracket myth: a tax deduction reduces taxable income (worth your marginal rate on each dollar) while a tax credit reduces tax owed dollar-for-dollar — credits are worth more; most filers take the standard deduction, making many 'write-offs' irrelevant to them; and a refund is not free money, it's your own overpayment returning. Also load-bearing: the IRS initiates contact by mail, not by threatening phone calls demanding gift cards. Each misconception has a real cost, from bad job decisions to scam losses.

do: Write a two-sentence explanation of deduction vs credit in your own words, then check it against the IRS definitions — teaching-back is the fastest test of understanding.

children.title: Free Filing Help

learn.summary: Legitimately free options exist and are underused: IRS Free File (guided software for incomes under the annual threshold, around $79,000-$84,000 in recent years), IRS Direct File (the IRS's own free e-filing tool, expanded to many states), and VITA/TCE sites offering free in-person preparation by IRS-certified volunteers for most people earning under about $64,000, with elders and limited-English speakers prioritized. Paid preparers and 'refund advance' products often cost hundreds for returns these programs handle free.

do: Check whether you qualify for IRS Free File or Direct File this year, and look up the nearest VITA site — write down what you (or someone you know) would save versus paid preparation.
